lesson.title: Keyword Arguments: Calling Functions by Name
lesson.summary: A keyword argument names the parameter it is meant to fill at the call site, so Python matches it by that name instead of by its position, making the call order-independent and self-explanatory.
lesson.body:
Arguments are the actual values handed to a function when it is called, and the function has to have some rule for matching each argument to the correct parameter. Keyword arguments give an explicit rule: write parameter_name=value in the call, and Python matches that value to the parameter with that exact name, no matter where it appears among the other arguments.

Consider def describe_pet(name, animal, age): print(f"{name} is a {age}-year-old {animal}."). Calling it with keywords, describe_pet(animal="dog", age=3, name="Rex"), still works correctly even though the arguments are listed in a completely different order than the parameters were defined in. Python looks at each name, animal, age, name, and slots the matching value into the matching parameter, producing "Rex is a 3-year-old dog." regardless of the order they were typed in the call.

There is a rule about mixing the two styles: positional arguments (matched by order) must come before any keyword arguments in a call. Once a keyword argument appears, everything after it must also be given as a keyword, because Python cannot go back to matching by position after it has started matching by name. Writing describe_pet(name="Rex", 3, "dog") is invalid and Python raises a SyntaxError, positional argument follows keyword argument, before the code even runs.

Positional and keyword arguments can also be combined safely, as long as that order rule is respected: describe_pet("Rex", animal="dog", age=3) is valid, since the one positional argument, "Rex", is listed first and fills name, while the remaining two are supplied by keyword. This mixing is common in practice, keeping the first argument or two positional when their meaning is obvious from context, while naming the rest explicitly.

Keyword arguments pair naturally with default parameters. Suppose def connect(host="localhost", port=80, timeout=30): only building the connection with a longer timeout, but keeping the default host and port, can be written as connect(timeout=5). There is no need to repeat "localhost" and 80 just to reach the third parameter, and no risk of miscounting positions in a long argument list. The call also reads clearly to another programmer: timeout=5 states its own meaning without anyone needing to check the function's parameter order.

Beyond convenience, keyword arguments make code more resistant to a very common bug: silently swapping two arguments of the same type. describe_pet("dog", "Rex", 3) would run without error yet assign name="dog" and animal="Rex", producing nonsense output, because positional matching trusts the order completely. Naming the arguments removes that risk entirely, at the small cost of a slightly longer call. Library and API functions with many optional settings are almost always called with keyword arguments for exactly this reason.
